texts: mixed: the harvest event, its agent, the date and the past tense all land, but two pieces strain. Bare 'salt-bloom' becomes a kind constant rather than a referent, so sentence 3's 'The salt-bloom' mints a second, unconnected symbol and nothing says the stuff harvested is the stuff that came off the stones; and 'at the new-moon spring tide' puts an event-noun into a time slot, which nothing licenses. Rewrite as 'On day 33 of Year 1, Coraline Ash harvested the salt-bloom during the new-moon spring tide.' — the definite mints one salt-bloom referent later sentences can reuse, and 'during' is the licensed word for nesting one eventuality inside another. (Separately, 'day 33 of Year 1' has no day-of-year slot in the time vocabulary and currently lands in a day-of-month-shaped slot; that is a translator-side gap your wording cannot fix.)

bad: 'the stones of the second pool' is recorded as spatial containment, but an of-genitive does not license that head — it takes the part-whole relation or the opaque possession link — so the parse asserts a containment your words never stated. Since you do mean the stones lying in the pool, say it with the containment preposition: 'Coraline Ash scraped the submerged stones in the second pool with a wooden scraper.' The rest is good: the stones become a group with a per-stone 'submerged' rule, and the wooden scraper is the instrument with its 'scraper' genus — only note that 'the second pool' has to rank the pool against the bare kind 'pool' for want of a stated dimension.

mixed: the event itself is right — 'came off the stones' is read as motion with the stones as the source, 'pale flakes' becomes a flake group with a per-flake 'pale' rule, and the past tense is on the event. What fails is the link back: because sentence 1 left the salt-bloom as a bare kind, this 'The salt-bloom' mints a fresh referent, so nothing connects it to what Coraline harvested. Rewriting sentence 1 to 'harvested the salt-bloom' repairs the chain with no change needed here.

good. the flakes correctly reuse the group introduced in the previous sentence, gathering leaves them unchanged so they take the moved-object role, and the fine net lands as the instrument with 'fine' kept as a separate property of the net rather than fused into a kind name.

good. the singular collective 'harvest party' acts as one participant with no spurious distribution to its members, bare 'pools' becomes a pool group taking part in the event, and 'at midnight' is stored as a plain named time.

good. the repetition is recorded as its own 'again' tag on this second rotation rather than being folded into the event, the party keeps the same symbol as in the previous sentence, and 'at the third watch' is stored as a named time constant like 'midnight' — its ordinal sits inside that constant, so it is not separately queryable if you ever want to ask which watch.

good. inspecting leaves the pools as they were so they take the unchanged-object role, the count of two rides on the pool group, and 'southern' is handed to each pool by a rule rather than asserted of the group as an object.

mixed: the denial itself is exactly right — both the group-level 'no blooming happened' and a per-pool denial, so no individual southern pool can be shown to have bloomed. What is not carried is the 'had': nothing orders the non-blooming against the inspection you just reported, because a negated past perfect has no settled treatment. If that timing matters, a plain past with the time stated outright parses cleanly: 'The two southern pools did not bloom that night.'

bad: 'took the whole night' is recorded as a duration measured in 'night' units, but 'night' is a time-of-day word, not a measure unit — it cannot convert to seconds or be compared with any other duration, and it collides with the time-slot sense of the same word, so the span is either mis-typed or has to be dropped. State the span as an interval using the licensed day-part words instead: 'The harvest ran from dusk until dawn.' (or, if you can give a figure, 'The harvest took ten hours.'). The coreference is right either way — 'The harvest' points back to the harvesting of sentence 1.
